\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{Canonical forms.}
The kernel pattern is computed by a single left-to-right scan maintaining a value-to-first-index dictionary: $O(n)$ expected time, $O(n)$ space. The ordered pattern is computed by sorting the distinct values and looking up each entry: $O(n\log n)$ time. Both are canonical in the strict sense, so equivalence testing---$\Sym$-conjugacy in the first case, order-isomorphism in the second---is a single comparison after preprocessing.

\paragraph{Enumeration.}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:fixed} and Theorem~\ref{thm:partitions}, renaming blocks $0,1,2,\dots$ in order of first appearance identifies patterns with \emph{restricted growth strings}: $g_1=0$ and $g_{i+1}\le1+\max(g_1,\dots,g_i)$. Depth-first enumeration of these produces all $B_n$ partitions in constant amortised time each. By Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre}, faces are enumerated as a partition together with one of the $k!$ orderings of its blocks.

\paragraph{Counting.}
The recursions
\[
  S(n+1,k+1)=(k+1)S(n,k+1)+S(n,k),\qquad B_{n+1}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}B_{n-i}
\]
compute the counts in $O(n^2)$ big-integer operations without enumeration.

\section{Applications}

\paragraph{Group theory.} Theorem~\ref{thm:orbits} identifies the orbit space of the diagonal symmetric-group action on $X^n$ with the partition lattice of $[n]$ truncated at $|X|$ blocks---the ``group acts on the alphabet'' companion of the usual P\'olya-theoretic count where the group acts on the positions.

\paragraph{Data processing.} Grouping a table by a tuple of keys computes exactly its kernel, and the canonical form above is the standard dictionary-encoding pass. Theorem~\ref{thm:complete} reads as a statement about pseudonymisation: relabelling destroys value identity and nothing else.

\paragraph{Clustering.} Clustering outputs are set partitions; their space is the $B_n$-element lattice ordered by refinement, which by Theorem~\ref{thm:orderdict} is the intersection lattice of the braid arrangement under reverse inclusion, with dimension (Theorem~\ref{thm:dim}) the number of free parameters of a one-value-per-cluster model.

\paragraph{Exchangeable random partitions.} The Chinese restaurant process, the Ewens sampling formula and Kingman's coalescent are distributions on precisely these $B_n$ patterns, with Theorem~\ref{thm:bellrec} as the normalising recursion.

\paragraph{Ranking with ties.} Theorem~\ref{thm:fubini} counts the outcomes of an $n$-contestant competition with ties allowed, and Theorem~\ref{thm:faceclass} says two score vectors are indistinguishable to any tie-tolerant criterion exactly when they lie in the same face; rank statistics are the functions constant on faces.

\paragraph{Arrangements and topology.} The braid arrangement is the running example of the theory: the Poincar\'e polynomial $\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}(1+it)$ of its complexified complement is computed from the lattice of Theorem~\ref{thm:flats}, its chamber count $n!$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:chambers}) is the order of the Coxeter group, and the faces counted in Theorem~\ref{thm:fubini} form the underlying set of the face monoid governing the Tsetlin library random walk.

\section{Discussion and future directions}

Three features of the development deserve emphasis. First, \emph{invariance is separated from counting}: the completeness proof never touches enumeration and vice versa, the bridge being the fixed-point characterisation of Proposition~\ref{prop:fixed}. Second, \emph{one model, two recursions}: Corollary~\ref{cor:bellstirling} reconciles the binomial and triangle recursions by exhibiting one family of objects that both count. Third, \emph{two levels of order}: the $\pat$ vs $\rank$ dichotomy maps exactly onto the flat vs face dichotomy, with ratio $k!$.

\begin{conjecture}[Signed kernel patterns]
For the type-$B_n$ reflection arrangement (hyperplanes $x_i=\pm x_j$ and $x_i=0$) the complete invariant of a point's face is the \emph{signed kernel pattern}: the kernel of $i\mapsto|x_i|$, together with the sign vector and the ordering of the resulting blocks. The flats should be counted by $\sum_k\binom{n}{k}\widetilde S(k)$, the type-$B$ Dowling/partition numbers $1,2,6,24,116,648$, and the faces by the type-$B$ ordered analogue.
\end{conjecture}

The reason to expect this is that the kernel pattern never used the linear structure of the index set, only the relation ``same value''; replacing it by ``same value up to the sign action of $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^n\rtimes\Sym(n)$'' should give completeness by literally the congruence argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:congr}, with all the extra content in the counting, where the Dowling recursion replaces the Stirling one in the delete-the-last-index scheme.

\begin{conjecture}[M\"obius rigidity]
The M\"obius function of an interval $[\hat0,\pi]$ in the refinement lattice of kernel patterns depends only on the block sizes: for blocks of sizes $b_1,\dots,b_k$ one has $\mu(\hat0,\pi)=\prod_t(-1)^{b_t-1}(b_t-1)!$, hence $\mu(\hat0,\hat1)=(-1)^{n-1}(n-1)!$ and characteristic polynomial $\chi(t)=t(t-1)\cdots(t-n+1)$, from which the chamber count $n!$ and the face count would follow by the standard finite-field and Zaslavsky arguments---an independent third route to the results of Sections 4 and 6.
\end{conjecture}

Further directions: (i) for a proper subgroup $G\le\Sym(X)$ the kernel pattern is only a coarse invariant, and the fibres of the map from $G$-orbits to patterns---a refinement of the theory of orbitals---measure its failure, as Proposition~\ref{prop:sharp} shows must happen; (ii) partition metrics used in clustering evaluation could be compared with the Euclidean geometry of the flats $L(p)$, for instance via principal angles; (iii) $B_n$ grows super-exponentially, so statistical applications need unranking and exact uniform sampling rather than enumeration, and Theorems~\ref{thm:bellrec} and~\ref{thm:fubini} supply precisely the recursions required, in $O(n^2)$ arithmetic.

\section{Conclusion}

The kernel pattern---replace each entry of a tuple by the position at which its value first occurred---is a small, computable object answering three classification problems at once. It is a complete invariant of the diagonal symmetric-group action on tuples over a finite alphabet, sharp in that no proper subgroup admits it. It is a canonical form for set partitions, counted with $k$ blocks by $S(n,k)$ and in total by $B_n=1,1,2,5,15,52,\dots$, its two decompositions reconciling the Bell and Stirling recursions. And it is a complete invariant of the flats of the braid arrangement, with dimension equal to block count. Refining by the ordering of blocks classifies faces instead of flats, multiplies each count by $k!$, and produces the ordered Bell numbers $1,1,3,13,75,541,\dots$, inside which the $n!$ chambers sit as the top stratum.

Self-contained numerical demonstration of the results:

     partitions of {0,...,n-1}.  Their number is the Bell number B_n
     (1, 1, 2, 5, 15, 52, ...), and those with k blocks number S(n,k).

  3. Geometry: the flat L(x) = { v in R^n : x_i = x_j => v_i = v_j } of the

Run:  python3 demo.py
Only the standard library is used.

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations, product
from math import comb, factorial
from typing import Dict, Hashable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Canonical forms
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def kernel_pattern(x: Sequence[Hashable]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """pat(x)_i = index of the first occurrence of the value x_i.  O(n)."""
    first: Dict[Hashable, int] = {}
    out: List[int] = []
    for i, value in enumerate(x):
        if value not in first:
            first[value] = i
        out.append(first[value])
    return tuple(out)


def ordered_pattern(v: Sequence[float]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """rank(v)_i = number of distinct values of v strictly below v_i.  O(n log n)."""
    order = {value: k for k, value in enumerate(sorted(set(v)))}
    return tuple(order[value] for value in v)


def blocks_of(p: Sequence[Hashable]) -> List[List[int]]:
    """The set partition induced by a tuple, blocks sorted by least element."""
    groups: Dict[Hashable, List[int]] = {}
    for i, value in enumerate(p):
        groups.setdefault(value, []).append(i)
    return sorted(groups.values(), key=min)


def is_pattern(p: Sequence[int]) -> bool:
    """Pointwise test: p is a kernel pattern iff p_i <= i and p_{p_i} = p_i."""
    return all(p[i] <= i for i in range(len(p))) and all(
        p[p[i]] == p[i] for i in range(len(p))
    )


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Completeness of the invariant: build the witnessing permutation
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def witness_permutation(
    x: Sequence[Hashable], y: Sequence[Hashable], alphabet: Sequence[Hashable]
) -> Dict[Hashable, Hashable] | None:
    """A permutation sigma of `alphabet` with sigma(x_i) = y_i for all i, or None.

    Implements the reconstruction proof: match used values via the tuples, then
    match the unused values by any bijection (possible since the alphabet is
    finite and the used parts are equinumerous).
    """
    if kernel_pattern(x) != kernel_pattern(y):
        return None
    sigma: Dict[Hashable, Hashable] = {}
    for a, b in zip(x, y):
        if a in sigma and sigma[a] != b:
            return None
        sigma[a] = b
    used_targets = set(sigma.values())
    free_sources = [a for a in alphabet if a not in sigma]
    free_targets = [b for b in alphabet if b not in used_targets]
    for a, b in zip(free_sources, free_targets):
        sigma[a] = b
    return sigma


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Enumeration and counting
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def all_patterns(n: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Every kernel pattern of length n, by restricted-growth-string search."""
    out: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []

    def extend(prefix: List[int]) -> None:
        if len(prefix) == n:
            out.append(tuple(prefix))
            return
        i = len(prefix)
        # the new index either opens a new block (representative i) or joins an
        # existing block, i.e. points at one of the representatives seen so far
        choices = sorted({prefix[j] for j in range(i)} | {i})
        for a in choices:
            prefix.append(a)
            extend(prefix)
            prefix.pop()

    extend([])
    return out


def all_ordered_patterns(n: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Every ordered pattern (weak order) of length n: partition + block order."""
    out: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []
    for p in all_patterns(n):
        blocks = blocks_of(p)
        for order in permutations(range(len(blocks))):
            r = [0] * n
            for position, block in zip(order, blocks):
                for i in block:
                    r[i] = position
            out.append(tuple(r))
    return out


def stirling_second(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """S(n,k) by the triangle recursion S(n+1,k+1) = (k+1)S(n,k+1) + S(n,k)."""
    table = [[0] * (k + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    if k >= 0:
        table[0][0] = 1
    for m in range(n):
        for j in range(min(m + 1, k) + 1):
            if j + 1 <= k:
                table[m + 1][j + 1] = (j + 1) * table[m][j + 1] + table[m][j]
    return table[n][k]


def bell(n: int) -> int:
    """B_n by the binomial recursion B_{n+1} = sum_i C(n,i) B_{n-i}."""
    values = [1]
    for m in range(n):
        values.append(sum(comb(m, i) * values[m - i] for i in range(m + 1)))
    return values[n]


def fubini(n: int) -> int:
    """Ordered Bell number a_n = sum_k S(n,k) k!."""
    return sum(stirling_second(n, k) * factorial(k) for k in range(n + 1))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Geometry of the braid arrangement
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def flat_basis(x: Sequence[Hashable]) -> List[List[float]]:
    """Basis of L(x) = {v : x_i = x_j => v_i = v_j}: block indicator vectors."""
    n = len(x)
    return [[1.0 if i in block else 0.0 for i in range(n)] for block in blocks_of(x)]


def flat_dimension(x: Sequence[Hashable]) -> int:
    """dim L(x) = number of blocks of the kernel of x."""
    return len(blocks_of(x))


def in_flat(v: Sequence[float], x: Sequence[Hashable]) -> bool:
    """Membership test for the flat cut out by x."""
    n = len(x)
    return all(v[i] == v[j] for i in range(n) for j in range(n) if x[i] == x[j])


def flats_equal(x: Sequence[Hashable], y: Sequence[Hashable]) -> bool:
    """L(x) = L(y), tested directly through the defining equations."""
    n = len(x)
    same_x = {(i, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(n) if x[i] == x[j]}
    same_y = {(i, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(n) if y[i] == y[j]}
    return same_x == same_y


def chamber_of(v: Sequence[float]) -> Tuple[int, ...] | None:
    """The permutation indexing the chamber of an injective vector, else None."""
    if len(set(v)) != len(v):
        return None
    return tuple(sorted(range(len(v)), key=lambda i: v[i]))


def same_face(v: Sequence[float], w: Sequence[float]) -> bool:
    """v and w lie in the same face iff they realise the same strict comparisons."""
    n = len(v)
    return all(
        (v[i] < v[j]) == (w[i] < w[j]) for i in range(n) for j in range(n)
    )

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations, product
from math import comb, factorial
from typing import Dict, Hashable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Canonical forms
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def kernel_pattern(x: Sequence[Hashable]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """pat(x)_i = index of the first occurrence of the value x_i.  O(n)."""
    first: Dict[Hashable, int] = {}
    out: List[int] = []
    for i, value in enumerate(x):
        if value not in first:
            first[value] = i
        out.append(first[value])
    return tuple(out)


def ordered_pattern(v: Sequence[float]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """rank(v)_i = number of distinct values of v strictly below v_i.  O(n log n)."""
    order = {value: k for k, value in enumerate(sorted(set(v)))}
    return tuple(order[value] for value in v)


def blocks_of(p: Sequence[Hashable]) -> List[List[int]]:
    """The set partition induced by a tuple, blocks sorted by least element."""
    groups: Dict[Hashable, List[int]] = {}
    for i, value in enumerate(p):
        groups.setdefault(value, []).append(i)
    return sorted(groups.values(), key=min)


def is_pattern(p: Sequence[int]) -> bool:
    """Pointwise test: p is a kernel pattern iff p_i <= i and p_{p_i} = p_i."""
    return all(p[i] <= i for i in range(len(p))) and all(
        p[p[i]] == p[i] for i in range(len(p))
    )


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Completeness of the invariant: build the witnessing permutation
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def witness_permutation(
    x: Sequence[Hashable], y: Sequence[Hashable], alphabet: Sequence[Hashable]
) -> Dict[Hashable, Hashable] | None:
    """A permutation sigma of `alphabet` with sigma(x_i) = y_i for all i, or None.

    Implements the reconstruction proof: match used values via the tuples, then
    match the unused values by any bijection (possible since the alphabet is
    finite and the used parts are equinumerous).
    """
    if kernel_pattern(x) != kernel_pattern(y):
        return None
    sigma: Dict[Hashable, Hashable] = {}
    for a, b in zip(x, y):
        if a in sigma and sigma[a] != b:
            return None
        sigma[a] = b
    used_targets = set(sigma.values())
    free_sources = [a for a in alphabet if a not in sigma]
    free_targets = [b for b in alphabet if b not in used_targets]
    for a, b in zip(free_sources, free_targets):
        sigma[a] = b
    return sigma


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Enumeration and counting
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def all_patterns(n: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Every kernel pattern of length n, by restricted-growth-string search."""
    out: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []

    def extend(prefix: List[int]) -> None:
        if len(prefix) == n:
            out.append(tuple(prefix))
            return
        i = len(prefix)
        # the new index either opens a new block (representative i) or joins an
        # existing block, i.e. points at one of the representatives seen so far
        choices = sorted({prefix[j] for j in range(i)} | {i})
        for a in choices:
            prefix.append(a)
            extend(prefix)
            prefix.pop()

    extend([])
    return out


def all_ordered_patterns(n: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Every ordered pattern (weak order) of length n: partition + block order."""
    out: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []
    for p in all_patterns(n):
        blocks = blocks_of(p)
        for order in permutations(range(len(blocks))):
            r = [0] * n
            for position, block in zip(order, blocks):
                for i in block:
                    r[i] = position
            out.append(tuple(r))
    return out


def stirling_second(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """S(n,k) by the triangle recursion S(n+1,k+1) = (k+1)S(n,k+1) + S(n,k)."""
    table = [[0] * (k + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    if k >= 0:
        table[0][0] = 1
    for m in range(n):
        for j in range(min(m + 1, k) + 1):
            if j + 1 <= k:
                table[m + 1][j + 1] = (j + 1) * table[m][j + 1] + table[m][j]
    return table[n][k]


def bell(n: int) -> int:
    """B_n by the binomial recursion B_{n+1} = sum_i C(n,i) B_{n-i}."""
    values = [1]
    for m in range(n):
        values.append(sum(comb(m, i) * values[m - i] for i in range(m + 1)))
    return values[n]


def fubini(n: int) -> int:
    """Ordered Bell number a_n = sum_k S(n,k) k!."""
    return sum(stirling_second(n, k) * factorial(k) for k in range(n + 1))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Geometry of the braid arrangement
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def flat_basis(x: Sequence[Hashable]) -> List[List[float]]:
    """Basis of L(x) = {v : x_i = x_j => v_i = v_j}: block indicator vectors."""
    n = len(x)
    return [[1.0 if i in block else 0.0 for i in range(n)] for block in blocks_of(x)]


def flat_dimension(x: Sequence[Hashable]) -> int:
    """dim L(x) = number of blocks of the kernel of x."""
    return len(blocks_of(x))


def in_flat(v: Sequence[float], x: Sequence[Hashable]) -> bool:
    """Membership test for the flat cut out by x."""
    n = len(x)
    return all(v[i] == v[j] for i in range(n) for j in range(n) if x[i] == x[j])


def flats_equal(x: Sequence[Hashable], y: Sequence[Hashable]) -> bool:
    """L(x) = L(y), tested directly through the defining equations."""
    n = len(x)
    same_x = {(i, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(n) if x[i] == x[j]}
    same_y = {(i, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(n) if y[i] == y[j]}
    return same_x == same_y


def chamber_of(v: Sequence[float]) -> Tuple[int, ...] | None:
    """The permutation indexing the chamber of an injective vector, else None."""
    if len(set(v)) != len(v):
        return None
    return tuple(sorted(range(len(v)), key=lambda i: v[i]))


def same_face(v: Sequence[float], w: Sequence[float]) -> bool:
    """v and w lie in the same face iff they realise the same strict comparisons."""
    n = len(v)
    return all(
        (v[i] < v[j]) == (w[i] < w[j]) for i in range(n) for j in range(n)
    )

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, Hashable, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple


def kernel_pattern(x: Sequence[Hashable]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Canonical form of a tuple under relabelling of the alphabet.

    pat(x)_i = index of the first occurrence of the value x_i.  One pass, O(n).
    """
    first: Dict[Hashable, int] = {}
    out: List[int] = []
    for i, value in enumerate(x):
        if value not in first:
            first[value] = i
        out.append(first[value])
    return tuple(out)


def same_orbit(x: Sequence[Hashable], y: Sequence[Hashable]) -> bool:
    """True iff some permutation of the alphabet carries x to y."""
    return kernel_pattern(x) == kernel_pattern(y)


def witness_permutation(
    x: Sequence[Hashable], y: Sequence[Hashable], alphabet: Sequence[Hashable]
) -> Optional[Dict[Hashable, Hashable]]:
    """An explicit permutation sigma of `alphabet` with sigma(x_i) = y_i, or None.

    Follows the reconstruction proof: the assignment x_i |-> y_i is well defined
    and injective on the values actually used (because the kernels agree), and
    the unused values are matched by any bijection between the two complements,
    which exist and are equinumerous because the alphabet is finite.
    """
    if kernel_pattern(x) != kernel_pattern(y):
        return None
    sigma: Dict[Hashable, Hashable] = {}
    for a, b in zip(x, y):
        if sigma.setdefault(a, b) != b:
            return None
    hit = set(sigma.values())
    free_src = [a for a in alphabet if a not in sigma]
    free_tgt = [b for b in alphabet if b not in hit]
    for a, b in zip(free_src, free_tgt):
        sigma[a] = b
    return sigma


def is_pattern(p: Sequence[int]) -> bool:
    """Pointwise membership test: p_i <= i and p_{p_i} = p_i."""
    return all(p[i] <= i for i in range(len(p))) and all(
        p[p[i]] == p[i] for i in range(len(p))
    )

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations
from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Tuple


def patterns(n: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Yield every kernel pattern of length n exactly once.

    Depth-first search over restricted growth: having fixed p_0,...,p_{i-1}, the
    next index either opens a new block (representative i) or joins an existing
    block, i.e. points at one of the representatives already used.  Constant
    amortised work per pattern; B_n patterns in total.
    """
    prefix: List[int] = []

    def extend() -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
        if len(prefix) == n:
            yield tuple(prefix)
            return
        i = len(prefix)
        for a in sorted(set(prefix) | {i}):
            prefix.append(a)
            yield from extend()
            prefix.pop()

    yield from extend()


def blocks_of(p: Tuple[int, ...]) -> List[List[int]]:
    """Blocks of a pattern, sorted by least element."""
    groups: Dict[int, List[int]] = {}
    for i, v in enumerate(p):
        groups.setdefault(v, []).append(i)
    return sorted(groups.values(), key=min)


def ordered_patterns(n: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Yield every ordered pattern (weak order) of length n exactly once.

    By the fibre theorem, the faces lying over a flat with k blocks are exactly
    the k! orderings of its blocks, so it suffices to enumerate patterns and,
    for each, all permutations of its blocks.
    """
    for p in patterns(n):
        bl = blocks_of(p)
        for order in permutations(range(len(bl))):
            r = [0] * n
            for position, block in zip(order, bl):
                for i in block:
                    r[i] = position
            yield tuple(r)


def flats_by_dimension(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """Count flats of the braid arrangement in R^n by dimension (= block count)."""
    counts = [0] * (n + 1)
    for p in patterns(n):
        counts[len(blocks_of(p))] += 1
    return counts

from __future__ import annotations

from math import comb, factorial
from typing import List


def stirling_triangle(n_max: int) -> List[List[int]]:
    """Rows S(n,0..n) for n <= n_max via S(n+1,k+1) = (k+1)S(n,k+1) + S(n,k).

    Derived from the delete-the-last-index dictionary: removing the final index
    either destroys a singleton block (leaving k blocks on n points) or leaves
    the block structure intact (k+1 blocks on n points, plus a choice of which
    block the removed index belonged to).  Cost: O(n^2) big-integer additions.
    """
    tri: List[List[int]] = [[1]]
    for n in range(1, n_max + 1):
        prev = tri[n - 1]
        row = [0] * (n + 1)
        for k in range(1, n + 1):
            row[k] = prev[k - 1] + k * (prev[k] if k < len(prev) else 0)
        tri.append(row)
    return tri


def bell_numbers(n_max: int) -> List[int]:
    """B_0..B_{n_max} via B_{n+1} = sum_i C(n,i) B_{n-i}.

    Derived by splitting a partition of n+1 points along the block of the last
    point: choosing that block's other |S| = i members in C(n,i) ways leaves an
    arbitrary partition of the remaining n-i points.  Cost: O(n^2).
    """
    bell = [1]
    for n in range(n_max):
        bell.append(sum(comb(n, i) * bell[n - i] for i in range(n + 1)))
    return bell


def fubini_numbers(n_max: int) -> List[int]:
    """Faces of the braid arrangement: a_n = sum_k S(n,k) k! (ordered Bell numbers)."""
    tri = stirling_triangle(n_max)
    return [
        sum(tri[n][k] * factorial(k) for k in range(n + 1)) for n in range(n_max + 1)
    ]


def check_identities(n_max: int = 12) -> bool:
    """Verify B_n = sum_k S(n,k), n! <= a_n and B_n <= a_n up to n_max."""
    tri = stirling_triangle(n_max)
    bell = bell_numbers(n_max)
    fub = fubini_numbers(n_max)
    return all(
        sum(tri[n]) == bell[n] and factorial(n) <= fub[n] and bell[n] <= fub[n]
        for n in range(n_max + 1)
    )

from math import factorial

def kernel_pattern(v: Sequence[Hashable]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """pat(v)_i = index of the first occurrence of the value v_i."""
    first: Dict[Hashable, int] = {}
    out: List[int] = []
    for i, value in enumerate(v):
        first.setdefault(value, i)
        out.append(first[value])
    return tuple(out)


def ordered_pattern(v: Sequence[float]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """rank(v)_i = number of distinct values of v strictly below v_i.  O(n log n)."""
    order = {value: k for k, value in enumerate(sorted(set(v)))}
    return tuple(order[value] for value in v)


def flat_data(v: Sequence[float]) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Full location of v in the braid arrangement.

    Returns the kernel pattern (naming the flat), the blocks, the dimension of

    p = kernel_pattern(v)
    groups: Dict[int, List[int]] = {}
    for i, a in enumerate(p):
        groups.setdefault(a, []).append(i)
    blocks = sorted(groups.values(), key=min)
    k = len(blocks)
    basis = [[1.0 if i in b else 0.0 for i in range(n)] for b in blocks]
    chamber: Optional[Tuple[int, ...]] = (
        tuple(sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: v[i])) if k == n else None
    )
    return {
        "kernel_pattern": p,
        "blocks": blocks,
        "dimension": k,
        "basis": basis,
        "ordered_pattern": ordered_pattern(v),

def all_patterns(n: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """All kernel patterns of length n (restricted growth search)."""
    out: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []

    def extend(prefix: List[int]) -> None:
        if len(prefix) == n:
            out.append(tuple(prefix))
            return
        i = len(prefix)
        for a in sorted(set(prefix) | {i}):
            prefix.append(a)
            extend(prefix)
            prefix.pop()

    extend([])
    return out


def blocks_of(p: Tuple[int, ...]) -> List[List[int]]:
    groups: Dict[int, List[int]] = {}
    for i, v in enumerate(p):
        groups.setdefault(v, []).append(i)
    return sorted(groups.values(), key=min)


def canonical(assignment: List[int]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Kernel pattern of an arbitrary block-labelling."""
    first: Dict[int, int] = {}
    out: List[int] = []
    for i, v in enumerate(assignment):
        first.setdefault(v, i)
        out.append(first[v])
    return tuple(out)


def merges(p: Tuple[int, ...]) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Partitions covering p: merge two blocks."""
    bl = blocks_of(p)
    out = []
    for a in range(len(bl)):
        for b in range(a + 1, len(bl)):
            lab = list(p)
            for i in bl[b]:
                lab[i] = p[bl[a][0]]
            out.append(canonical(lab))
    return out


def label(p: Tuple[int, ...]) -> str:
    return "|".join("".join(str(i) for i in b) for b in blocks_of(p))

<script>
const PALETTE = ["#7bdff2","#f7d488","#ffa8a8","#b197fc","#8ce99a","#ffd6a5","#a5d8ff","#ffc9de"];

function pat(t){const first={},out=[];t.forEach((v,i)=>{if(!(v in first))first[v]=i;out.push(first[v]);});return out;}
function blocksOf(t){const g={};t.forEach((v,i)=>{(g[v]=g[v]||[]).push(i);});
  return Object.values(g).sort((a,b)=>a[0]-b[0]);}
function rank(t){const vals=[...new Set(t)].sort((a,b)=>a-b);return t.map(v=>vals.indexOf(v));}
function factorial(n){let r=1;for(let i=2;i<=n;i++)r*=i;return r;}
function stirlingTable(n){const T=[[1]];
  for(let m=1;m<=n;m++){T[m]=[];for(let j=0;j<=m;j++){
    const a=(j>0)?T[m-1][j-1]:0, b=(j<=m-1)?T[m-1][j]:0; T[m][j]=a+j*b;}}

function stirling(n,k){if(k<0||k>n)return 0;return stirlingTable(n)[n][k];}

function fubini(n){const T=stirlingTable(n);let s=0;for(let k=0;k<=n;k++)s+=T[n][k]*factorial(k);return s;}

  document.getElementById('idem').innerHTML =
    JSON.stringify(pat(p))===JSON.stringify(p)

  document.getElementById('blocks').textContent =
    bl.map(function(b){return '{'+b.join(',')+'}';}).join(' ') || 'empty';
  document.getElementById('rank').textContent='('+r.join(', ')+')';
  const eqs = bl.filter(function(b){return b.length>1;})
                .map(function(b){return b.map(function(i){return 'v'+i;}).join(' = ');}).join(', ');
  document.getElementById('flat').innerHTML =
    'L(x) = { v in R<sup>'+n+'</sup> : '+(eqs || 'no conditions')+' }';
  document.getElementById('dim').textContent=k;
  document.getElementById('basis').innerHTML =
    bl.map(function(b){
      let row=[];for(let i=0;i<n;i++)row.push(b.indexOf(i)>=0?1:0);
      return '['+row.join(' ')+']';}).join('<br>');
  document.getElementById('n').textContent=n;
  document.getElementById('bn').textContent=bell(n);
  document.getElementById('snk').textContent=stirling(n,k);
  document.getElementById('kfact').textContent=factorial(k);
  document.getElementById('fub').textContent=fubini(n);
  document.getElementById('nfact').textContent=factorial(n);
  drawDiagram(bl,n);
}

function drawDiagram(bl,n){
  const svg=document.getElementById('diagram');
  const W=720,pad=60,y=140;
  const step=n>1?(W-2*pad)/(n-1):0;
  let s='';
  bl.forEach(function(b,bi){
    const col=PALETTE[bi%PALETTE.length];
    for(let t=0;t+1<b.length;t++){
      const x1=pad+b[t]*step,x2=pad+b[t+1]*step,h=30+18*Math.min(4,b.length);
      s+='<path d="M '+x1+' '+y+' Q '+((x1+x2)/2)+' '+(y-h)+' '+x2+' '+y+

    }
    b.forEach(function(i){
      const cx=pad+i*step;
      s+='<circle cx="'+cx+'" cy="'+y+'" r="13" fill="'+col+'" />';

      s+='<text x="'+cx+'" y="'+(y+36)+'" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#9aa3c7">'+b[0]+'</text>';

}

function randomise(){x=x.map(function(){return Math.floor(Math.random()*3);});

function relabel(){
  const vals=[...new Set(x)];

  const map={};vals.forEach(function(v,i){map[v]=pool[i];});

function merge(){
  const vals=[...new Set(x)];
  if(vals.length<2){note('Need at least two distinct values to merge.');return;}
  const before=JSON.stringify(pat(x));
  x=x.map(function(v){return v===vals[1]?vals[0]:v;});
  note('Non-injective recolouring. Pattern before '+before+', after '+JSON.stringify(pat(x))+
       ' — it must change, because coincidences were created.');
  render();
}
function addCell(){if(x.length<8){x.push(0);note('');render();}}
function removeCell(){if(x.length>1){x.pop();note('');render();}}
function reset(){x=[0,1,0,2,1];note('');render();}
function note(m){document.getElementById('note').textContent=m;}
render();
</script>

<div class="wrap">

<script>
const cv=document.getElementById('cv'),ctx=cv.getContext('2d');
const W=cv.width,H=cv.height,CX=W/2,CY=H/2,SC=170;
// orthonormal basis of the plane v0+v1+v2 = 0
const E1=[1/Math.SQRT2,-1/Math.SQRT2,0];
const E2=[1/Math.sqrt(6),1/Math.sqrt(6),-2/Math.sqrt(6)];
let tol=0.06, mouse={a:0.9,b:0.35};

function toVec(a,b){return [a*E1[0]+b*E2[0], a*E1[1]+b*E2[1], a*E1[2]+b*E2[2]];}
function screenOf(a,b){return [CX+SC*a, CY-SC*b];}
function planeOf(px,py){return [(px-CX)/SC, (CY-py)/SC];}

function classify(v){
  // blocks under |v_i - v_j| < tol
  const idx=[0,1,2], parent=[0,1,2];
  function find(i){while(parent[i]!==i)i=parent[i];return i;}
  function uni(i,j){parent[find(i)]=find(j);}
  for(let i=0;i<3;i++)for(let j=i+1;j<3;j++) if(Math.abs(v[i]-v[j])<tol) uni(i,j);
  const groups={};
  idx.forEach(function(i){const r=find(i);(groups[r]=groups[r]||[]).push(i);});
  const blocks=Object.values(groups).sort(function(a,b){return a[0]-b[0];});
  const pat=[0,0,0];
  blocks.forEach(function(b){b.forEach(function(i){pat[i]=b[0];});});
  // block value = mean, then rank the blocks
  const vals=blocks.map(function(b){let s=0;b.forEach(function(i){s+=v[i];});return s/b.length;});
  const sorted=vals.slice().sort(function(p,q){return p-q;});
  const rank=[0,0,0];
  blocks.forEach(function(b,bi){b.forEach(function(i){rank[i]=sorted.indexOf(vals[bi]);});});
  return {blocks:blocks,pat:pat,rank:rank};
}

function orderString(v,c){
  const items=[0,1,2].slice().sort(function(i,j){return c.rank[i]-c.rank[j];});
  let s='v'+items[0];
  for(let t=1;t<3;t++) s += (c.rank[items[t]]===c.rank[items[t-1]] ? ' = ' : ' < ')+'v'+items[t];

  "interactive_layout": "# Kernel Patterns: the Shape of Sameness

*A guided tour from a five-bead necklace to the face structure of one of the most-studied
objects in geometry.*

---

## 1. One question, three subjects

Take a list of five things — say five coloured beads:

$$\text{red},\ \text{blue},\ \text{red},\ \text{green},\ \text{blue}.$$

Now forget the colours, but keep one fact: **which positions carry the same thing as which**.
Position $1$ matches position $3$; position $2$ matches position $5$; position $4$ is alone.

The cleanest way to write that down is to replace each entry by the position at which its value
*first appeared*:

$$\operatorname{pat}(x)_i \;=\; \min\{\,j : x_j = x_i \,\}, \qquad\text{here}\quad (1,2,1,4,2).$$

This is the **kernel pattern**. It is going to answer three questions at once:

| question | subject | answer |
|---|---|---|
| when are two tuples the same up to relabelling the alphabet? | algebra | same kernel pattern |
| how many set partitions does an $n$-set have? | combinatorics | the Bell number $B_n$ |
| what are the flats and faces of the arrangement $\{v_i = v_j\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$? | geometry | patterns, and ordered patterns |

Play with the first one before reading any further.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

> **Try this.** Press *Relabel alphabet (bijective)* several times: the tiles change colour but the
> kernel pattern in the first box never moves. Then press *Merge two values*: the pattern jumps
> immediately. That contrast is the whole first theorem.

---

## 2. The invariance theorem, and why it is not obvious

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the formal statements and their proofs</b></summary>

**Value stability.** $x_{\operatorname{pat}(x)_i} = x_i$, because $\operatorname{pat}(x)_i$ is by
construction a member of $\{j : x_j = x_i\}$.

**Faithfulness.** $\operatorname{pat}(x)_i = \operatorname{pat}(x)_j \iff x_i = x_j$.
Left to right: $x_i = x_{\operatorname{pat}(x)_i} = x_{\operatorname{pat}(x)_j} = x_j$.
Right to left: the two sets whose minima define the two values coincide.

**Kernel congruence.** If $x_k = x_l \iff y_k = y_l$ for all $k,l$, then
$\operatorname{pat}(x) = \operatorname{pat}(y)$. Indeed $y_{\operatorname{pat}(y)_i} = y_i$
transfers to $x_{\operatorname{pat}(y)_i} = x_i$, so $\operatorname{pat}(x)_i \le \operatorname{pat}(y)_i$;
symmetrise.

**Invariance.** If $f$ is injective, $\operatorname{pat}(f\circ x) = \operatorname{pat}(x)$, since
injectivity gives $f(x_k) = f(x_l) \iff x_k = x_l$. In particular the pattern is unchanged by any
permutation of the alphabet.

**Idempotence.** $\operatorname{pat}(\operatorname{pat}(x)) = \operatorname{pat}(x)$: the tuple and
its pattern have the same kernel.

**Which tuples are patterns?** Exactly those $p$ with $p_i \le i$ and $p_{p_i} = p_i$ — weakly
regressive and idempotent. This is the test the widget above runs live.
</details>

Invariance is the easy half. The prize is **completeness**: patterns do not merely fail to
distinguish tuples in the same orbit; they distinguish everything else.

> **Completeness Theorem.** Let $X$ be a finite set and $x,y \in X^n$. There is a permutation
> $\sigma$ of $X$ with $\sigma \circ x = y$ **if and only if** $\operatorname{pat}(x) = \operatorname{pat}(y)$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the reconstruction argument (it is constructive)</b></summary>

Equal patterns mean $x_i = x_j \iff y_i = y_j$. So the assignment $x_i \mapsto y_i$ is well defined
and injective on $S = \operatorname{im}(x)$, and surjective onto $T = \operatorname{im}(y)$: it is a
bijection $S \to T$. Since $X$ is finite and $|S| = |T|$, the complements $X\setminus S$ and
$X\setminus T$ have the same size, so pick any bijection between them and glue. The result is a
permutation $\sigma$ of $X$ with $\sigma\circ x = y$.

**Sharpness.** Both hypotheses matter. Over $X = \{0,1\}$ the one-entry tuples $(0)$ and $(1)$ have
the same pattern, but the *trivial* subgroup of $\operatorname{Sym}(X)$ cannot carry one to the
other: for a proper subgroup the kernel is no longer a complete invariant.
</details>

The algorithm below is the proof made executable: it computes canonical forms in one pass and, when
two tuples match, hands back an explicit permutation witnessing it.

{{algorithm:0}}

---

## 3. Counting: patterns *are* set partitions

A kernel pattern is exactly a way of splitting $\{1,\dots,n\}$ into groups, with each group named
after its smallest member. So counting patterns is counting **set partitions**, and the answer is
the [Bell numbers](https://oeis.org/A000110)

$$1,\ 1,\ 2,\ 5,\ 15,\ 52,\ 203,\ 877,\ 4140,\ \dots$$

There are two proofs, and they are different in kind.

*The finite check.* Patterns are the fixed points of $\operatorname{pat}$, so for small $n$ you can
simply sift all $n^n$ tuples: $1, 1, 2, 5, 15, 52$. Certain, but silent about $n = 6$.

*The recursion.* Look at the block containing the last index, say $S \cup \{n+1\}$, and delete it;
what remains is an **arbitrary** partition of the complement, and the construction reverses. Grouping
the subsets $S$ by size:

$$B_{n+1} \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i} B_{n-i}.$$

Run the same delete-the-last-index idea one level finer — the last index is either alone in its
block, or inside one of the $k$ existing blocks — and you get the
[Stirling numbers of the second kind](https://oeis.org/A008277)

$$S(n+1,k+1) \;=\; (k+1)S(n,k+1) + S(n,k),$$

counting the patterns with exactly $k$ blocks. Summing over $k$:

$$B_n \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{n} S(n,k).$$

That identity is worth staring at. The Bell recursion and the Stirling recursion never mention one
another; the identity is true because both are counting kernel patterns, sliced two different ways.

{{algorithm:2}}

Enumeration, as opposed to counting, is done by [restricted growth strings](https://oeis.org/A000110):

## 4. The same story in $\mathbb{R}^n$

Here is where it gets geometric. In $\mathbb{R}^n$, consider the **braid arrangement** — the family
of hyperplanes

$$H_{ij} = \{v : v_i = v_j\}, \qquad i<j,$$

the mirrors of the transpositions in the symmetric group. Intersecting some of them gives a **flat**;
a flat is the set of vectors that are *constant on the blocks of a partition*. So flats are
partitions, and partitions are patterns:

> **Geometric Classification.** For a tuple $x$ let $L(x) = \{v : x_i = x_j \Rightarrow v_i = v_j\}$.
> Then $L(x) = L(y)$ iff $\operatorname{pat}(x) = \operatorname{pat}(y)$; inclusion $L(x)\subseteq L(y)$
> is refinement of kernels, order-reversingly; and $\dim L(x)$ is the number of blocks.
>
> Consequently the intersection lattice of the braid arrangement in $\mathbb{R}^n$ has exactly
> $B_n$ elements, with $S(n,k)$ of dimension $k$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click for the two short proofs</b></summary>

*Inclusion is refinement.* If $L(x)\subseteq L(y)$ and $y_i = y_j$, apply the containment to the
**block indicator** $\mathbf{1}^x_i$ (the vector with a $1$ in every position of $i$'s block): its
$i$- and $j$-coordinates must agree, and the $i$-coordinate is $1$, forcing $x_j = x_i$.

*Dimension is block count.* A vector constant on blocks is exactly a free choice of one real number
per block, so restriction to block representatives is an isomorphism
$L(x) \cong \mathbb{R}^{\#\text{blocks}}$.
</details>

The lattice for $n = 4$ — $15$ flats in rows of $1, 7, 6, 1$, which are $S(4,1),\dots,S(4,4)$:

{{visualization:1}}

## 5. Adding order: faces, chambers, and a second sequence

The kernel pattern forgets the *order* of the values. Put it back:

$$\operatorname{rank}(v)_i \;=\; \#\{\text{distinct values of } v \text{ strictly below } v_i\}.$$

For $v = (3.1, 7.0, 3.1, -2.0, 7.0)$ the distinct values are $-2.0 < 3.1 < 7.0$, so
$\operatorname{rank}(v) = (1,2,1,0,2)$. This records the whole weak order and nothing else: it is
unchanged by any strictly increasing reparametrisation of the value line.

Geometrically it names the **face** — the relatively open cone cut out by the full system of
comparisons — rather than the flat.

> **Face Classification.** $F(v) = F(w)$ iff $\operatorname{rank}(v) = \operatorname{rank}(w)$, where
> $F(v) = \{w : v_i<v_j \iff w_i<w_j\}$. Faces are convex. The top-dimensional faces are the
> **chambers** $v_{\sigma(1)} < \cdots < v_{\sigma(n)}$, one for each permutation, so there are $n!$ of them.

The next widget lets you walk around the whole arrangement for $n=3$ and watch both invariants
change together. The plane drawn is $v_0+v_1+v_2 = 0$; the three yellow lines are the mirrors.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

> **Try this.** Hover inside a coloured region: three blocks, dimension $3$, an open chamber.
> Cross a yellow line — widening the tolerance slider makes this easy — and two coordinates merge:
> the kernel pattern loses a block and the dimension drops to $2$. Head for the centre and everything
> merges: the diagonal line $v_0=v_1=v_2$, dimension $1$. Six chambers, six rays, one origin:
> $13$ faces in total.

Why $13$? Because of the counting step that ties the two halves together:

> **Fibre Theorem.** A flat with $k$ blocks carries exactly $k!$ faces — one for each ordering of its
> blocks. Hence
> $$\#\{\text{faces}\} \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^n S(n,k)\,k!,$$
> the [ordered Bell (Fubini) numbers](https://oeis.org/A000670) $1, 1, 3, 13, 75, 541, \dots$

For $n=3$: $1\cdot 1! + 3\cdot 2! + 1\cdot 3! = 1 + 6 + 6 = 13$. For $n=5$: $52$ flats, $120$ chambers,
$541$ faces. And two inequalities fall straight out — $n! \le a_n$ because the chambers are a single
term of the sum, and $B_n \le a_n$ because $k! \ge 1$ term by term. Geometrically: every chamber is a
face, and every flat carries at least one.

{{algorithm:3}}

## 6. How fast do the three censuses grow?

{{visualization:0}}

The Bell numbers grow faster than $c^n$ for every constant $c$ but slower than $n!$; the Fubini
numbers dominate both. The heat map on the right is the Stirling triangle: its row sums are the flat
counts, its factorially-weighted row sums are the face counts.

---

## 8. Where this shows up

- **Databases.** A `GROUP BY` on a tuple of keys computes precisely its kernel; the one-pass canonical
  form is the standard dictionary-encoding step. Completeness says pseudonymisation destroys value
  identity and nothing else.
- **Clustering.** Clustering outputs live in exactly this $B_n$-element lattice ordered by refinement —
  the intersection lattice under reverse inclusion — and the number of clusters is the dimension of the
  corresponding flat, i.e. the number of free parameters left.
- **Exchangeable random partitions.** The [Chinese restaurant process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_restaurant_process),
  the Ewens sampling formula and Kingman's coalescent are probability distributions on these $B_n$
  patterns, normalised by the Bell recursion.
- **Ranking with ties.** The Fubini numbers count the outcomes of an $n$-runner race with ties allowed;
  two score vectors are indistinguishable to any tie-tolerant criterion exactly when they share a face.
- **Topology of arrangements.** The [braid arrangement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrangement_of_hyperplanes)
  is *the* running example: its complexified complement classifies the pure braid group, its chamber
  count $n!$ is the order of the Coxeter group, and its face poset carries the face-monoid random walks.

---

## 9. What to try next

<details>
<summary><b>Open problems the same machinery should reach</b></summary>

**Signed kernel patterns.** For the type-$B$ reflection arrangement (hyperplanes $x_i = \pm x_j$ and
$x_i = 0$), the conjectured complete invariant is the kernel of $i \mapsto |x_i|$ together with the
sign vector and the ordering of blocks; the flats should be counted by $\sum_k \binom{n}{k}\widetilde S(k)$,
the type-$B$ Dowling numbers $1,2,6,24,116,648$. The invariance half should go through by literally the
same congruence argument — all the new content is in the counting.

**Möbius rigidity.** The Möbius function of the refinement lattice should depend only on block sizes:
$\mu(\hat0,\pi) = \prod_t (-1)^{b_t-1}(b_t-1)!$, hence characteristic polynomial
$t(t-1)\cdots(t-n+1)$ — from which the chamber and face counts would follow a third, independent way.

**Beyond the full symmetric group.** For a proper subgroup $G$ the kernel pattern is only a coarse
invariant; measuring the fibres of "$G$-orbits $\to$ patterns" refines the theory of orbitals.
</details>

The moral, in one line: **coincidence structure is the invariant content of a tuple**, and once you
make it canonical, the algebra, the enumeration and the geometry are three readings of one object.

/-!
# Kernel patterns of tuples: a complete invariant for the symmetric-group action

For a tuple `x : Fin n → X` its *kernel* is the equivalence relation
`i ~ j ↔ x i = x j` on the index set `Fin n`.  We encode it by the canonical
*pattern* `pat x : Fin n → Fin n`, sending `i` to the least index `j` with
`x j = x i` (the "first occurrence" representative).

Main results of this file.

* `pat_eq_iff` — `pat` faithfully records the kernel.
* `pat_congr`, `pat_comp_injective` — `pat` is invariant under post-composition
  by injective maps, in particular under the diagonal action of `Equiv.Perm X`.
* `exists_perm_of_pat_eq`, `perm_orbit_iff_pat_eq` — for a *finite* value type
  `X`, equality of patterns is *exactly* equality of `Sym(X)`-orbits, i.e. the
  kernel is a complete invariant of the symmetric-group action on `X ^ n`.
* `pat_not_complete_of_trivial_group` — sharpness: for a proper subgroup the
  kernel need not be a complete invariant.
* `pat_idem`, `mem_patterns_iff` — patterns are exactly the idempotent tuples
  `p : Fin n → Fin n` with `pat p = p`; consequently the set of patterns
  *stabilises*: `patterns n m = patterns n n` as soon as `n ≤ m`
  (`patterns_stabilise`).
-/

namespace Geometry.KernelPatterns

open Finset

variable {n : ℕ} {X Y : Type*}

section Pat

variable [DecidableEq X]

/-- The *kernel pattern* of a tuple `x : Fin n → X`: the index `pat x i` is the
least `j` with `x j = x i`. -/
def pat (x : Fin n → X) (i : Fin n) : Fin n :=
  (univ.filter fun j => x j = x i).min' ⟨i, by simp⟩

lemma pat_mem (x : Fin n → X) (i : Fin n) :
    pat x i ∈ univ.filter fun j => x j = x i := Finset.min'_mem _ _

@[simp] lemma apply_pat (x : Fin n → X) (i : Fin n) : x (pat x i) = x i := by
  have := pat_mem x i; simpa using this

lemma pat_le (x : Fin n → X) (i : Fin n) : pat x i ≤ i :=
  Finset.min'_le _ _ (by simp)

/-- Two tuples with the same kernel have the same pattern. -/
lemma pat_congr [DecidableEq Y] {x : Fin n → X} {y : Fin n → Y}
    (h : ∀ k l, x k = x l ↔ y k = y l) : pat x = pat y := by
  funext i
  apply le_antisymm
  · exact Finset.min'_le _ _ (by simpa using (h _ _).2 (apply_pat y i))
  · exact Finset.min'_le _ _ (by simpa using (h _ _).1 (apply_pat x i))

/-- The pattern records the kernel faithfully. -/
@[simp] lemma pat_eq_iff {x : Fin n → X} {i j : Fin n} :
    pat x i = pat x j ↔ x i = x j := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    calc x i = x (pat x i) := (apply_pat x i).symm
      _ = x (pat x j) := by rw [h]
      _ = x j := apply_pat x j
  · intro h
    apply le_antisymm
    · exact Finset.min'_le _ _ (by simp [h])
    · exact Finset.min'_le _ _ (by simp [h])

/-- `pat` is invariant under post-composition with an injective map: it is a
`Sym(X)`-invariant (indeed an invariant for all of `X ↪ Y`). -/
lemma pat_comp_injective [DecidableEq Y] {f : X → Y} (hf : Function.Injective f)
    (x : Fin n → X) : pat (f ∘ x) = pat x :=
  (pat_congr (fun _ _ => by simp [hf.eq_iff])).symm

@[simp] lemma pat_perm (σ : Equiv.Perm X) (x : Fin n → X) : pat (σ ∘ x) = pat x :=
  pat_comp_injective σ.injective x

/-- The first-occurrence representative is a fixed point of the pattern map. -/
@[simp] lemma pat_apply_pat (x : Fin n → X) (i : Fin n) : pat x (pat x i) = pat x i :=
  pat_eq_iff.2 (apply_pat x i)

/-- Patterns are idempotent. -/
@[simp] lemma pat_idem (x : Fin n → X) : pat (pat x) = pat x :=
  pat_congr (fun _ _ => pat_eq_iff)

end Pat

/-! ### Completeness of the invariant for the symmetric group -/

section Complete

variable [Fintype X] [DecidableEq X]

/-- If two tuples over a finite type have equal patterns then some permutation
of the value type carries one to the other. -/
theorem exists_perm_of_pat_eq {x y : Fin n → X} (h : pat x = pat y) :
    ∃ σ : Equiv.Perm X, σ ∘ x = y := by
  classical
  have hxy : ∀ i j, x i = x j ↔ y i = y j := by
    intro i j
    rw [← pat_eq_iff (x := x), ← pat_eq_iff (x := y), h]
  set S : Set X := Set.range x with hS
  set T : Set X := Set.range y with hT
  let φ : S → T := fun a => ⟨y (Classical.choose a.2), Set.mem_range_self _⟩
  have hφ : ∀ a : S, x (Classical.choose a.2) = (a : X) := fun a => Classical.choose_spec a.2
  have hinj : Function.Injective φ := by
    intro a b hab
    have h1 : y (Classical.choose a.2) = y (Classical.choose b.2) := congrArg Subtype.val hab
    have h2 := (hxy _ _).2 h1
    exact Subtype.ext (by rw [← hφ a, ← hφ b]; exact h2)
  have hsurj : Function.Surjective φ := by
    intro b
    obtain ⟨j, hj⟩ := b.2
    refine ⟨⟨x j, Set.mem_range_self j⟩, Subtype.ext ?_⟩
    have hx : x (Classical.choose (⟨x j, Set.mem_range_self j⟩ : S).2) = x j := hφ _
    simpa [φ, hj] using (hxy _ _).1 hx
  let e : S ≃ T := Equiv.ofBijective φ ⟨hinj, hsurj⟩
  have hcard : Fintype.card (Sᶜ : Set X) = Fintype.card (Tᶜ : Set X) := by
    rw [Fintype.card_compl_set, Fintype.card_compl_set, Fintype.card_congr e]
  let e' : (Sᶜ : Set X) ≃ (Tᶜ : Set X) := Fintype.equivOfCardEq hcard
  refine ⟨(Equiv.Set.sumCompl S).symm.trans ((e.sumCongr e').trans (Equiv.Set.sumCompl T)), ?_⟩
  funext i
  have hmem : x i ∈ S := Set.mem_range_self i
  simp only [Function.comp_apply, Equiv.trans_apply,
    Equiv.Set.sumCompl_symm_apply_of_mem hmem, Equiv.sumCongr_apply, Sum.map_inl,
    Equiv.Set.sumCompl_apply_inl]
  have hval : (e ⟨x i, hmem⟩ : X) = y (Classical.choose (⟨x i, hmem⟩ : S).2) := rfl
  rw [hval]
  exact (hxy _ _).1 (hφ ⟨x i, hmem⟩)

/-- **Kernel patterns are a complete `Sym(X)`-invariant.** -/
theorem perm_orbit_iff_pat_eq (x y : Fin n → X) :
    (∃ σ : Equiv.Perm X, σ ∘ x = y) ↔ pat x = pat y := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨σ, rfl⟩; exact (pat_perm σ x).symm
  · exact exists_perm_of_pat_eq

end Complete

/-- Sharpness: for the trivial subgroup of `Sym(Fin 2)` the kernel is *not* a
complete invariant — the tuples `![0]` and `![1]` share a pattern but lie in
different orbits. -/
theorem pat_not_complete_of_trivial_group :
    pat (![0] : Fin 1 → Fin 2) = pat ![1] ∧
      ¬ ∃ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin 2), σ ∈ (⊥ : Subgroup (Equiv.Perm (Fin 2))) ∧
        σ ∘ (![0] : Fin 1 → Fin 2) = ![1] := by
  constructor
  · decide
  · rintro ⟨σ, hσ, hcomp⟩
    rw [Subgroup.mem_bot] at hσ
    subst hσ
    have := congrFun hcomp 0
    simp at this

/-! ### The set of patterns, and stabilisation -/

/-- The finset of all kernel patterns of `n`-tuples with values in `Fin m`. -/
def patterns (n m : ℕ) : Finset (Fin n → Fin n) :=
  (univ : Finset (Fin n → Fin m)).image pat

/-- A tuple `p : Fin n → Fin n` is the pattern of some `Fin m`-valued tuple iff
it is idempotent and uses at most `m` distinct values. -/
lemma mem_patterns_iff {n m : ℕ} (p : Fin n → Fin n) :
    p ∈ patterns n m ↔ pat p = p ∧ (univ.image p).card ≤ m := by

# Kernel patterns as the flats of the braid arrangement

The braid arrangement `A_{n-1}` in `ℝ^n` is the family of hyperplanes
`H_{ij} = {v | v i = v j}`.  Its *flats* (the elements of its intersection
lattice) are the subspaces obtained by intersecting families of these
hyperplanes; each such subspace is cut out by the equations coming from an
equivalence relation on the index set.

* `braidFlat x` — the flat cut out by the kernel of the tuple `x`.
* `braidFlat_eq_iff` — **two tuples cut out the same flat iff they have the
  same kernel pattern**, so `pat` is a complete invariant of the flat.
* `braidFlat_le_iff` — the (order-reversing) dictionary between inclusion of
  flats and refinement of kernels.
* `finrank_braidFlat` — the dimension of the flat is the number of blocks.
* `card_braidFlats` — the intersection lattice of the braid arrangement has
  exactly `(patterns n n).card` elements; for `n ≤ 5` this is the Bell number
  (`card_braidFlats_five : ... = 52`).

open Finset

variable {n : ℕ} {X : Type*}

/-- The flat of the braid arrangement determined by the kernel of a tuple `x`:
the set of vectors constant on the blocks of `x`. -/
def braidFlat (x : Fin n → X) : Submodule ℝ (Fin n → ℝ) where
  carrier := {v | ∀ i j, x i = x j → v i = v j}
  add_mem' := by intro a b ha hb i j h; simp [ha i j h, hb i j h]
  zero_mem' := by intro i j _; rfl
  smul_mem' := by intro c a ha i j h; simp [ha i j h]

    v ∈ braidFlat x ↔ ∀ i j, x i = x j → v i = v j := Iff.rfl

/-- The characteristic vector of the block of `i`. -/
def blockIndicator [DecidableEq X] (x : Fin n → X) (i : Fin n) : Fin n → ℝ :=
  fun k => if x k = x i then 1 else 0

lemma blockIndicator_mem [DecidableEq X] (x : Fin n → X) (i : Fin n) :
    blockIndicator x i ∈ braidFlat x := by
  intro k l h
  simp [blockIndicator, h]

/-- Inclusion of flats is refinement of kernels (order-reversingly). -/
theorem braidFlat_le_iff [DecidableEq X] {Y : Type*} [DecidableEq Y]

    by_contra hx
    rw [if_neg fun hji => hx hji.symm] at hval
    exact one_ne_zero hval
  · intro h v hv i j hy
    exact hv i j (h i j hy)

/-- **The flat is a complete geometric encoding of the kernel pattern.** -/
theorem braidFlat_eq_iff [DecidableEq X] {Y : Type*} [DecidableEq Y]

  constructor
  · intro h
    refine pat_congr fun k l => ?_
    have h1 := (braidFlat_le_iff y x).1 h.ge
    have h2 := (braidFlat_le_iff x y).1 h.le
    exact ⟨fun hkl => h1 k l hkl, fun hkl => h2 k l hkl⟩

      intro i j
      rw [← pat_eq_iff (x := x), ← pat_eq_iff (x := y), h]

    · exact (braidFlat_le_iff x y).2 fun i j hy => (hker i j).2 hy
    · exact (braidFlat_le_iff y x).2 fun i j hx => (hker i j).1 hx

/-!
# Cycle 2: ordered patterns and the faces of the braid arrangement

A kernel pattern remembers which coordinates of a tuple agree; an *ordered*
pattern also remembers how the resulting blocks are ordered.  Geometrically,
kernel patterns index the flats of the braid arrangement while ordered patterns
index its **faces** (relatively open cones): the face containing `v` is cut out
by the full system of comparisons `v i ≤ v j`.

  canonical form of an ordered pattern.
* `rank_lt_iff`, `rank_eq_iff` — `rank` records the weak order faithfully.
* `rank_congr`, `rank_comp_strictMono` — ordered patterns are invariant under
  strictly monotone reparametrisation of the values, i.e. they are the
  invariants of the action of the order-automorphisms of the value line.
* `face_eq_iff` — two tuples span the same face iff they have the same ordered
  pattern; `face_convex`; a chamber is the face of an injective tuple
  (`face_eq_chamber`).
* `card_ordPatterns_le_four` — the face counts `1, 1, 3, 13, 75`, the
  ordered Bell (Fubini) numbers OEIS A000670.

open Finset

variable {n : ℕ} {X : Type*} [LinearOrder X]

/-! ### The ordered pattern (rank function) -/

/-- The rank of the coordinate `i`: the number of blocks of `v` carrying a
value strictly smaller than `v i`. -/
def rank (v : Fin n → X) (i : Fin n) : Fin n :=
  ⟨(univ.filter fun j => pat v j = j ∧ v j < v i).card, by
    have h1 : pat v i ∉ (univ.filter fun j => pat v j = j ∧ v j < v i) := by
      simp [apply_pat]
    have h2 : (univ.filter fun j => pat v j = j ∧ v j < v i) ⊂ univ :=
      ⟨Finset.subset_univ _, fun h => h1 (h (Finset.mem_univ _))⟩
    simpa using Finset.card_lt_card h2⟩

lemma rank_val (v : Fin n → X) (i : Fin n) :
    (rank v i : ℕ) = (univ.filter fun j => pat v j = j ∧ v j < v i).card := rfl

/-- The rank function is strictly monotone with respect to the values. -/
theorem rank_lt_iff {v : Fin n → X} {i j : Fin n} : rank v i < rank v j ↔ v i < v j := by

    omega
  · intro h

    · exact absurd (rank_lt_iff.1 hgt) (by rw [h]; exact lt_irrefl _)

      · exact absurd ((h j i).2 hgt) (by rw [hij]; exact lt_irrefl _)
    · intro hij

def chamber (n : ℕ) (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) : Set (Fin n → ℝ) :=

theorem chamber_convex (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) : Convex ℝ (chamber n σ) := by

    rcases eq_or_lt_of_le ha with ha0 | hapos
    · have hb1 : b = 1 := by linarith
      have ha1 : a = 0 := ha0.symm

/-! ### Counting -/

/-- Transport of the partition count along a bijection of index types. -/
noncomputable def setoidCongr {α β : Type*} (e : α ≃ β) : Setoid α ≃ Setoid β where
  toFun s := s.comap e.symm
  invFun s := s.comap e
  left_inv s := by
    refine Setoid.ext fun a b => ?_
    show s.r (e.symm (e a)) (e.symm (e b)) ↔ s.r a b
    simp
  right_inv s := by
    refine Setoid.ext fun a b => ?_
    show s.r (e (e.symm a)) (e (e.symm b)) ↔ s.r a b
    simp

  rw [← Nat.card_eq_finsetCard, Nat.card_congr (patternsEquivSetoid m)]

    Nat.card (Setoid α) = (patterns (Fintype.card α) (Fintype.card α)).card := by
  rw [Nat.card_congr (setoidCongr (Fintype.equivFin α)), card_setoid_eq_card_patterns]

  have h1 : (lastBlkFibre n S).card = Nat.card (Setoid ↥(Sᶜ)) := by
    rw [← Nat.card_eq_finsetCard, Nat.card_congr (lastBlkFibreEquiv n S)]
  rw [h1, card_setoid_of_card_eq]
  congr 2 <;> · rw [Fintype.card_coe, Finset.card_compl]; simp

/-- Fibring the patterns of `Fin (n+1)` over the block of the last index. -/
theorem card_patterns_succ_eq_sum (n : ℕ) :
    (patterns (n + 1) (n + 1)).card
      = ∑ S : Finset (Fin n), (patterns (n - S.card) (n - S.card)).card := by
  rw [Finset.card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise
    (f := fun p : Fin (n + 1) → Fin (n + 1) => lastBlk p)
    (t := (univ : Finset (Finset (Fin n)))) (fun p _ => Finset.mem_coe.2 (Finset.mem_univ _))]
  exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun S _ => card_lastBlkFibre n S

theorem sum_subsets_eq_sum_choose (n : ℕ) (f : ℕ → ℕ) :
    ∑ S : Finset (Fin n), f S.card = ∑ i ∈ range (n + 1), n.choose i * f i := by
  have h := Finset.sum_powerset_apply_card f (x := (univ : Finset (Fin n)))
  rw [Finset.powerset_univ] at h
  simpa [smul_eq_mul] using h

theorem card_patterns_succ (n : ℕ) :
    (patterns (n + 1) (n + 1)).card
      = ∑ i ∈ range (n + 1), n.choose i * (patterns (n - i) (n - i)).card := by
  rw [card_patterns_succ_eq_sum]
  exact sum_subsets_eq_sum_choose n fun i => (patterns (n - i) (n - i)).card

theorem card_patterns_eq_bell : ∀ n : ℕ, (patterns n n).card = Nat.bell n
  | 0 => by rw [card_patterns_zero, Nat.bell_zero]
  | n + 1 => by

/-!
# Kernel patterns with a prescribed number of blocks are the Stirling numbers

Mathlib defines the Stirling numbers of the second kind `Nat.stirlingSecond`
purely by their recursion.  Here we prove that they really do count kernel
patterns: the number of equality patterns of `n`-tuples having exactly `k`
distinct values is `Nat.stirlingSecond n k`
(`card_patternsWith_eq_stirlingSecond`).

The proof is a structural induction implemented by an explicit
restriction/extension dictionary between patterns on `Fin (n+1)` and patterns on
`Fin n`:

* `restr p` — delete the last index;
* `extend q a` — re-attach a last index whose representative is `a`;
* `extend_restr`, `restr_extend` — these are mutually inverse.

Deleting the last index either destroys a singleton block (`p` fixes the last
index) or leaves the block structure unchanged (`p` sends it into one of the
`k` existing blocks), which is exactly the Stirling recursion
`S(n+1, k+1) = (k+1) * S(n, k+1) + S(n, k)`.

namespace Geometry.KernelPatterns

open Finset

variable {n : ℕ}

/-! ### A pointwise characterisation of patterns -/

/-- A tuple `p : Fin n → Fin n` is its own pattern exactly when it is a
"choice of least representatives": weakly decreasing on indices and
idempotent. -/
theorem pat_eq_self_iff (p : Fin n → Fin n) :
    pat p = p ↔ (∀ i, p i ≤ i) ∧ ∀ i, p (p i) = p i := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    refine ⟨fun i => ?_, fun i => ?_⟩
    · have hi := pat_le p i
      rwa [h] at hi
    · have hi := pat_apply_pat p i
      rwa [h] at hi
  · rintro ⟨hle, hidem⟩
    funext i
    apply le_antisymm
    · exact Finset.min'_le _ _ (by simp [hidem i])
    · refine Finset.le_min' _ _ _ ?_
      intro j hj
      simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and] at hj
      calc p i = p j := hj.symm
        _ ≤ j := hle j

    p ∈ patternsWith n k ↔ pat p = p ∧ (univ.image p).card = k := by
  simp [patternsWith, mem_patterns_self]

/-! ### Deleting and re-attaching the last index -/

/-- Delete the last index from a pattern on `Fin (n+1)`. -/
def restr (p : Fin (n + 1) → Fin (n + 1)) (i : Fin n) : Fin n :=
  if h : (p i.castSucc : ℕ) < n then ⟨p i.castSucc, h⟩ else i

/-- Re-attach a last index to a pattern on `Fin n`, with representative `a`. -/
def extend (q : Fin n → Fin n) (a : Fin (n + 1)) : Fin (n + 1) → Fin (n + 1) :=
  fun j => if h : (j : ℕ) < n then (q ⟨j, h⟩).castSucc else a

@[simp] lemma extend_castSucc (q : Fin n → Fin n) (a : Fin (n + 1)) (i : Fin n) :
    extend q a i.castSucc = (q i).castSucc := by
  simp only [extend, Fin.val_castSucc, i.isLt, dif_pos]

    extend q a (Fin.last n) = a := by

    restr (extend q a) = q := by

  rw [dif_pos (q i).isLt]

    have h1 : (restr p i : ℕ) = (p i.castSucc : ℕ) := restr_apply_val hp i

  · rcases Fin.eq_castSucc_or_eq_last j with ⟨i, rfl⟩ | rfl
    · rw [extend_castSucc]
      exact Fin.castSucc_le_castSucc_iff.2 (hle i)
    · rw [extend_last]
      exact Fin.le_last a
  · rcases Fin.eq_castSucc_or_eq_last j with ⟨i, rfl⟩ | rfl
    · rw [extend_castSucc, extend_castSucc, hidem]
    · rw [extend_last]
      rcases ha with rfl | ⟨w, hw, rfl⟩
      · rw [extend_last]
      · rw [extend_castSucc, hw]

    simp only [Finset.mem_filter, mem_patternsWith] at hp

/-- **The Stirling recursion for kernel patterns.** -/
theorem card_patternsWith_succ_succ (n k : ℕ) :
    (patternsWith (n + 1) (k + 1)).card
      = (k + 1) * (patternsWith n (k + 1)).card + (patternsWith n k).card := by
  classical
  have hsplit := Finset.card_filter_add_card_filter_not
    (s := patternsWith (n + 1) (k + 1)) (p := fun p => p (Fin.last n) = Fin.last n)
  rw [card_patternsWith_fixing_last, card_patternsWith_moving_last] at hsplit
  omega

/-! ### Base cases and the identification with `Nat.stirlingSecond` -/

theorem card_patternsWith_zero_zero : (patternsWith 0 0).card = 1 := by decide

theorem card_patternsWith_zero_succ (k : ℕ) : (patternsWith 0 (k + 1)).card = 0 := by
  rw [Finset.card_eq_zero]
  ext p
  simp [mem_patternsWith]

theorem card_patternsWith_succ_zero (n : ℕ) : (patternsWith (n + 1) 0).card = 0 := by
  rw [Finset.card_eq_zero]
  ext p
  simp only [mem_patternsWith, Finset.notMem_empty, iff_false, not_and]
  intro _
  have hne : (univ.image p).Nonempty := ⟨p 0, Finset.mem_image_of_mem _ (Finset.mem_univ 0)⟩

second kind.**  This links Mathlib's recursively defined `Nat.stirlingSecond` to
an actual count of set partitions. -/
theorem card_patternsWith_eq_stirlingSecond :
    ∀ n k : ℕ, (patternsWith n k).card = Nat.stirlingSecond n k
  | 0, 0 => by rw [card_patternsWith_zero_zero, Nat.stirlingSecond_zero]
  | 0, _ + 1 => by rw [card_patternsWith_zero_succ, Nat.stirlingSecond_zero_succ]
  | _ + 1, 0 => by rw [card_patternsWith_succ_zero, Nat.stirlingSecond_succ_zero]

      rw [card_patternsWith_succ_succ, Nat.stirlingSecond_succ_succ,
        card_patternsWith_eq_stirlingSecond n (k + 1), card_patternsWith_eq_stirlingSecond n k]

theorem card_patterns_eq_sum_stirlingSecond (n : ℕ) :
    (patterns n n).card = ∑ k ∈ range (n + 1), Nat.stirlingSecond n k := by
  rw [card_patterns_eq_sum_blocks]
  exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun k _ => card_patternsWith_eq_stirlingSecond n k
